newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-In with the old, out with the young at FCL.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-In with the old, out with the young at FCL.

text.p: It was out with the young and in with the old as New Zealand conglomerate Fletcher Challenge Ltd announced leadership changes on Wednesday.
Chief executive Hugh Fletcher, 50, announced he will retire in December and be replaced by Michael Andrews, seven years his senior.
Andrews, currently chief executive of Fletcher Challenge Energy and Fletcher Challenge Forests, has been appointed against the wishes of some market analysts who wanted an outside appointment.
He is very much an insider. In his 27 years with FCL he had headed virtually every division of the company -- forestry, building materials, steel, rural and energy.
Andrews told Reuters he beat out an international field of 50 contestants whom the board has been interviewing for months.
He said his track record points to why he won the position.

It was under his leadership that FCL won bids on two major privatisations -- for the Rural Bank, which was taken from under the noses of several leading banks, and the central North Island forests, which was won last year for NZ$2.0 billion (US$1.35 billion) from Carter Holt Harvey, the front-runner controlled by International Paper.
Andrews said he was also responsible for rapidly turning FCL into the world's biggest methanol producer and then quitting the industry in short order for a substantial profit.
Fletcher, grandson of the company founder Sir James Fletcher, had always said he wanted to stay chief executive for only 10 years so someone with fresh ideas could come in.
He will remain on the board and is almost certain to take over as chairman from Sir Ronald Trotter.
Andrews agrees it is ironic that he is the older man.
"But you are as old as you feel and I don't feel too old at all," he said.
On a four-year contract, he rejects suggestions that he is merely a caretaker.
"I've never been a caretaker, it's not my style. A lot can be achieved in four years and a lot will be achieved," he said.
When he starts at the end of the year, Andrews said, there will be no dramatic changes as he has been intimately connected to most of FCL's decision-making already.

"The role is primarily one of providing vision for the four divisions, helping in terms of the development of strategy, ensuring they are developing the right people and ensuring senior managers are well managed," he said.
Andrews said that none of the four divisions particularly needs attention although he admits that the shortness of the upswing in the pulp cycle this time around was a concern.
"We are working on how we should manage cycles."
Part of his role will be to manage his "portfolio" and he said selling troublesome Canadian pulp and paper assets is always on the agenda.
"We have to look at all options and look at the portfolio of pulp and paper assets around the world and that's always on the top of the list."
Andrews said the break-up of the company 16 months ago into four separate listed divisions had greatly helped FCL realise value for shareholders and there is more to come.
"I don't think the market valued our energy assets or the performance of those assets in the conglomerate stock. It's probably true in the other stocks.
"It's improving but I think there is some way to go."
But he disagrees that the company would be better off completely broken up into its composite parts.

He said FCL was able to buy methanol interests in Chile via its forest interests there, to buy gas in Canada from having forests there and to get involved with China's Citic in the North Island forest privatisation after working with the Chinese in Fletcher Steel.
"To leverage those things, it would be impossible to do that if the divisions were split out and went their own way.
"We believe the position we are in has created enormous value to shareholders and there is more to come yet."
